column3: Spending from what one loves and God's knowledge of it clarify the quality and evaluation of giving.
It specifies that the good spent in 2:272 should come from wholesome earnings and produce.
Seeking the Lord's face directly reinforces the required intention in 2:272.
Withholding is against one's own self, explaining why spending is for the giver's own benefit.
Forgiving a debtor in hardship gives a concrete form of charitable release.
It repeats that what is spent will be fully repaid and no wrong will be done.
It frames spending by God's ownership and distinguishes degrees of giving.
Each soul being fully repaid without wrong supports the promised return in 2:272.
The image of straight walking gives an indirect parallel to guidance.
It identifies needy recipients and again states that God knows every good spent.
It names fear of poverty as an obstacle to giving and counters it with God's promise.
Seeking the Lord's bounty and remembering His guidance has a limited link to turning toward God.
It states that one cannot guide whom one loves; God guides whom He wills.
It completes the giving context through open or hidden charity directed to the poor.
It names the recipients of good spending and affirms God's knowledge of every good deed.
It joins charity with seeking God's approval, supporting the intention criterion.
God's accounting of what is hidden within supports the importance of the giver's intention.
The command to compete in good gives a general horizon for spending.
It rejects preventing support and recalls that the stores of provision belong to God.
Wisdom as abundant good has only a limited connection to charitable good.
Giving wealth despite loving it to those in need broadens the ethical content of good spending.
Seeking God's face through giving and receiving increase joins intention with return.
Its rule against wronging or being wronged supports the justice at 2:272's close.
It refers to guidance from God but has no giving context.
Eagerness for their guidance does not grant the power to guide them.
God's knowledge of every expenditure supports the assurance of divine recompense.
Every soul's full repayment without wrong confirms 2:272's conclusion.
It combines seeking the Lord's face with secret and public spending, making the intention concrete.
It promises reward and freedom from fear for secret and public spending at all times.
Feeding solely for God's face, without seeking return or thanks, directly explains 2:272.
Fulfilling contracts adds no element to the explanation of guidance or spending here.
Faith and obedience give a broad framework of turning to God, not a direct spending link.
Righteous deeds being good provides only a general value framework for spending.
Giving oneself in pursuit of God's approval supports the selfless direction of intention.
The distinction between usury and trade supplies nearby financial context but only indirectly.
Full payment of wages and the absence of wrong support 2:272's promise.
God's favor to whom He wills is a limited parallel to divine choice in guidance.
God's growth of charities explains why giving is good for the giver in the nearby context.
It presents spending from God's provision within devoted worship.
Human willing being subject to God's will is a general frame for the guidance statement.
What a soul earns returning to it supports the claim that spending is for yourselves.
Abraham's fulfillment adds no clear element to guidance or spending in 2:272.
Attachment to wealth in tension with guidance indirectly illuminates an obstacle to giving.
Reward and freedom from fear for believers who give zakah support the recompense theme.
The superiority of the night adds nothing to the explanation of guidance or spending.
Giving the due of kin, the needy, and the traveler is joined to seeking God's face.
Leaving usury continues the surrounding moral order for wealth, indirectly.
It gives a standard of acceptance in devotion but does not explain spending in 2:272.
The warning about ambiguous verses adds no explanation of guidance or spending here.
Justice and safeguards in debt have an indirect connection to not wronging in financial dealings.
Divine judgment and return are too remote from 2:272's specific themes.
Human willing being within God's will is a general parallel to divine guidance.
God's knowledge of entrusted dealings and testimony has a limited link to divine knowledge.
The later life being better adds no direct explanation of giving or guidance.
Building upon God's approval offers a general parallel to sound intention.
It places spending from God's provision within the practice of worship.
The rebuke for disputing without knowledge does not explain giving or guidance here.
Full repayment for deeds without wrong supports 2:272's final assurance.
Following the best revelation has a general link to guidance but does not explain spending.
Covenant keeping and God-loving the mindful only distantly connect to intention and return.
God clarifying what to guard after guidance supports guidance as divine action.
Using what God gave for the hereafter and doing good broadens the direction of spending.
Creation and God's incomparability add no element to 2:272's guidance or spending.
Spending to seek God's approval and strengthen oneself directly opens 2:272.
The smallness of worldly enjoyment and no wrong being done is a remote parallel to recompense.
Rejecting another god adds no direct explanation of the guidance and spending context.
People wronging themselves connects from the opposite direction to the assurance of no wrong.
No one can mislead one whom God guides, reinforcing that guidance belongs to God alone.
God guides whom He wills to a straight path, supporting 2:272's guidance statement.
Taking full measure has only a remote link to avoiding wrong.
Not bearing responsibility for another's purification approaches the limit on responsibility for guidance.
Following the messenger in order to be guided generally complements the guidance distinction.
God not guiding the defiantly disobedient supports guidance as a divine judgment.
The one given good provision spends from it secretly and openly, showing giving from means.
Following the best word and God's guidance is a general contribution to the guidance theme.
Guidance joined to faith free of wrong gives an indirect moral measure.
The enduring face of the Lord illuminates the exalted object sought in giving for God's face.
Seeking God's bounty and giving thanks has an indirect link to provision and beneficence.
The prior warning adds no clear element to giving or responsibility for guidance.
God not guiding those who reject His signs supports guidance as His divine judgment.
The depiction of food in punishment does not develop 2:272's meaning.
Good advanced for oneself and found with God reinforces both personal benefit and recompense.
The messenger's task is only delivery while God's task is account, clarifying the limit of responsibility.
God's full payment supports the assurance of complete recompense in general.
God's knowledge of what is hidden gives a remote parallel to divine knowledge of intention.
Mistaking inherited practice for guidance indirectly shows that true guidance is not a human claim.
The Lord's great bounty gives a general link to the grace behind recompense.
Each person spends according to what was given, and no soul is burdened beyond that.
Spending is good for yourselves and protection from inner stinginess, directly repeating 2:272.
Fulfilling vows and circumambulation add no explanation of guidance or spending here.
Feeding a needy person and voluntary good being better for oneself support giving's personal return.
Seeking God's bounty and giving thanks only indirectly relate to provision.
God's knowledge beyond human knowledge is a general parallel to the divine side of guidance.
Revelation guiding to a path is a general but distant contribution to guidance.
God's knowledge and the clarification of limits only indirectly relate to intention and divine knowledge.
A plea for charity amid hardship illustrates giving's relief of need.
God giving His bounty to whom He wills has a limited link to divine will and guidance.
The image of radiant faces adds no clear element to guidance or spending.
God granting abundance to whom He wills indirectly relates to provision and divine choice.
God's willing to clarify, guide, and turn toward people generally supports divine agency in guidance.
Good sent ahead for yourselves is found with God, directly matching personal benefit and return.
Spending is joined to doing good and avoiding self-destruction, giving a broader ethical frame.
It answers what to spend with surplus, supplying a direct measure for voluntary giving.
The good loan to God is multiplied, strongly supporting divine repayment for spending.
It commands spending before a day without exchange or intercession, adding urgency to the call.
The parable of multiplied grain directly develops the return on spending in God's path.
Giving without reminder or injury preserves reward, fearlessness, and grieflessness.
A kind word and forgiveness surpass charity followed by injury, qualifying how giving is made.
Showy giving and harm nullify charity, sharply clarifying the required Godward intention.
The ruined garden parable warns against rendering one's charitable work fruitless.
Spending in ease and hardship broadens the giver's commitment beyond surplus conditions.
Miserliness with God's bounty is shown to harm its holder, reinforcing that withholding turns back on oneself.
Spending to be seen by people supplies the direct opposite of spending for God's face.
Faith and spending from God's provision present the positive alternative to showy giving.
God does not wrong even an atom's weight and multiplies good, strongly supporting 2:272's justice and return.
A good loan to God is linked with multiplied recompense and forgiveness.
Giving the due on harvest day supplies a concrete provision-based form of spending.
Hoarding wealth instead of spending in God's path gives the contrary warning to 2:272's generosity.
Unaccepted spending exposes that outward giving without a sound stance is not sufficient.
It specifies the designated recipients and public uses of charitable dues.
Some spending is sought as nearness to God, directly supporting Godward intention.
It rejects compelling people to believe, closely reinforcing that another's guidance is not the messenger's burden.
Whoever is guided is guided for his own self, directly paralleling personal benefit in 2:272.
It commands secret and open spending before the final day, extending the pattern of giving.
It commands giving the due of kin, the needy, and the traveler, expanding the recipient side.
When unable to give, a gentle word preserves the ethical relation to those seeking provision.
It warns against both clenched withholding and reckless overextension, balancing expenditure.
It includes spending from God's provision among the marks of humble, God-conscious people.
It joins establishing prayer and giving zakah within the community's religious duty.
It commands those with abundance to give and forgive, extending generosity beyond strict entitlement.
It names charitable men and women among those promised forgiveness and great reward.
Whatever is spent is replaced by God, directly reinforcing the assurance of return.
Secret and public spending from provision is described as a trade that does not fail.
The command to spend from God's provision meets the objection that God could feed the needy Himself, directly clarifying giver responsibility.
Spending from provision is listed among the practices of the faithful community.
Stinginess when wealth is requested exposes that withholding is against one's own self.
The asker and deprived person have a recognized claim in the wealth of the righteous.
Spending from wealth held in succession frames possessions as entrusted rather than absolute ownership.
A good loan to God is multiplied and rewarded generously, directly supporting divine repayment.
Charitable men and women are promised multiplication and a noble reward.
Charity before private consultation is presented as purer, linking giving with purification.
It directs wealth away from circulation only among the rich, supplying a social purpose for transfer.
Giving others preference despite personal need powerfully develops selfless generosity.
Spending in God's path is part of the saving response of faith.
It urges spending before death, when a person will wish to give charity too late.
A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, directly joining giving with divine return.
The righteous set aside a known right in their wealth, making giving an established obligation to others.
It identifies that established right as belonging to the asker and the deprived.
Feeding the needy, orphan, and captive supplies the concrete act explained by 76:9's Godward intention.
Giving with mindfulness and affirming the best prepares the way of ease, linking generosity to moral direction.
The most God-conscious person is described as one who gives wealth, adding the broader counterpart to 92:20.
Giving wealth for self-purification directly supports the claim that spending benefits the giver.
Giving without seeking repayment for a favor sharpens the absence of recipient-directed return.
The giver's eventual contentment completes the reward horizon of the nearby intention passage.
Not repelling the petitioner supplies an interpersonal counterpart to charitable responsiveness.
Sincere devotion directed solely to God gives a general foundation for the intention in 2:272.
